opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest thing I learned from Jensen is that when you face a problem, the natural human reaction is to explain why it's hard. You say, "We don't have enough GPUs," or "The data isn't there yet," or "This team is too small." All of those may be true, but Jensen tends to push back on that framing. His attitude is basically: okay, those are the constraints, now what are you going to do about it?

Early in my career, as a researcher, I would often frame things as "this didn't work because of X." That feels like analysis, but a lot of the time it's actually a way of protecting yourself. Being around Jensen, I noticed he doesn't really accept that as an endpoint. He wants to go back to first principles. What is the real limit here? Is it physics, or is it just that we haven't tried hard enough or thought about it the right way? Very often it turns out the barrier isn't fundamental. It's just uncomfortable to push through.

So it changed my mindset. Now when my team runs into something, I try not to start with why it can't be done. I start by asking what it would take to get it done. If we need more compute, how do we make the case for it? If the data doesn't exist, can we generate it, maybe with simulation or with our own models? That's partly how we think about world models and physical AI. The data problem is real, but instead of using it as an excuse, you treat it as the problem you're actually there to solve.

There's also an ownership aspect. Excuses usually point outside yourself, to the environment, other teams, the resources. Jensen's way of thinking pulls it back to you. If it matters, you own it. That's demanding, honestly, but it's also freeing, because you stop waiting for perfect conditions and just start moving.

r001.rationale: The response says that if more compute is needed, the team should make the case for it, and that if the data is missing, they should generate it; it also says, “If it matters, you own it.”

r002.rationale: The response describes Jensen’s approach and its effect on the speaker, but does not attribute that effect to Huang’s stature.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest shift for me came from watching how Jensen handles problems. At NVIDIA, when something isn't working, the instinct a lot of us have as researchers is to explain why. The data wasn't ready, the compute wasn't allocated, the other team didn't deliver on time. And those explanations are often true. But Jensen has this very simple attitude: he doesn't really care about the reasons. He cares about whether the problem gets solved.

I remember early on, I would come into a meeting with a very well-prepared story about why we were behind. And he would just cut through it. Not in a harsh way, but he'd say something like, okay, so what are you going to do about it? The excuse itself has no value to him. It doesn't move anything forward.

At first that was uncomfortable, because as a scientist you're trained to analyze causes. But over time I realized the difference between analyzing a cause and making an excuse. Analyzing a cause is about finding the path forward. An excuse is about protecting yourself. Jensen only has patience for the first one.

So now, when I hit a wall with my team, I try to catch myself. If I notice I'm constructing a narrative about why something is not my fault, I stop. I ask instead: if there were no excuses allowed, what would I do right now? Usually there's an answer. Maybe it's not the ideal answer, maybe it means working harder or going around an obstacle in an ugly way, but there is almost always something you can do.

He also models it himself. When NVIDIA makes a mistake, he says we made a mistake, we're fixing it, and he moves on. There's no long justification. That kind of ownership from the very top makes it hard for anyone below to hide behind reasons. It changed how I lead, honestly. I try to be the person who says, this is where we are, this is what I'm doing next, rather than the person who explains why we're not where we wanted to be.

r001.rationale: The response says to focus on what one can do next and take ownership, but does not clearly say that securing the conditions needed to solve the problem is the solver’s responsibility.

r002.rationale: It describes Huang’s approach and says his ownership at the top affects others, but does not attribute the advice’s unusually strong impact to his stature.

astra-6.text: The way I think about it is that explaining why a problem is hard doesn’t solve it. You can have perfectly reasonable explanations for why something isn’t working, but you still have to ask, “What can I do next?” That’s the shift: acknowledge the constraints, then put your energy into finding a way forward.

r002.rationale: The response does not attribute the advice’s impact to Jensen Huang’s stature.

sol-6.1.text: He changed my thinking from explaining why something is difficult to asking what we can do about it. You can have perfectly reasonable explanations for why a problem hasn’t been solved, but those explanations don’t move you forward. The constraints may be real. The question is: what are you going to try next? For me, that’s the shift—spending less energy defending why something didn’t work and more energy finding a way to make it work.
